picks.title: This app makes the Pixel 11's HiLight feature actually useful
picks.excerpt: Third-party devs reverse-engineered control of the Pixel 11 Pro's HiLight hardware, turning a locked-down flagship feature into a programmable creative tool. A live example of users redesigning a device affordance the vendor shipped closed.
picks.rationale: A shipped hardware affordance gets reopened by outsiders — the clearest recent case of users out-designing the vendor's own feature scope.

picks.title: Exclusive: Inside the Pixel Watch 5's breathing emergency detection — and why it's like an 'airbag on your wrist'
picks.excerpt: Google's PM explains how on-wrist ML detects a breathing emergency and escalates without user input, plus new blood-pressure and insulin-resistance trends. A look at designing AI that must act silently and only when it matters.
picks.rationale: A product manager walking through how you design an AI that stays invisible until it has to save someone — the hardest interaction brief in wearables.

picks.title: XREAL AURA Surpasses 10,000 Unit Reservations Ahead of Launch This Fall
picks.excerpt: XREAL says the first Android XR AR glasses have topped 10,000 global reservations across consumers, developers and enterprise ahead of a $199 launch — an early demand signal for display glasses outside Meta's ecosystem.
picks.rationale: First real demand number for Android XR glasses, at a price that decides whether designers get a second AR platform to build for.

picks.title: New 'HomePad' reveal is another reason to put it in every room of your house
picks.excerpt: Apple's rumored HomePad will reportedly borrow Apple Watch-style customizable faces — an interface decision that treats an always-on AI home display as an ambient object first and an assistant second.
picks.rationale: Apple answering the ambient-display question with watch faces rather than a chat surface — a concrete stance on what an always-on AI screen should look like.

picks.title: Google built a camera-based tool to estimate body fat more accurately than wearables
picks.excerpt: Google Research says a photo-based body composition model beats smartwatch and smart-scale estimates — suggesting the phone camera, not the sensor-laden wearable, may become the health-tracking input.
picks.rationale: If a camera beats the sensor, the hardware you design around health data changes — the phone quietly displaces the wearable as the input device.
